title: POC Weekly Sync - Benchmark Review vs Baseline
summary: Weekly POC sync to review benchmark results comparing Redwood Dedicated hosted variant vs baseline provider. Discussed latency p50/p95, throughput, cost per 1k tokens, tuning steps (batching, quantization, cache settings), and next steps to validate p95 in production-like traffic. Action items assigned for follow-up runs and documentation sharing.
topics: next steps: productionlike test and security docs
next_steps: Alex to rerun p95 benchmark with batch_size=8 + int8 quantized model and share results by 2025-02-18
Maya to send updated pricing delta sheet and dedicated capacity options by 2025-02-17
Rachel to provide sample traffic profile (seq len distribution) by 2025-02-16
Schedule 1hr production-like load test for week of 2025-02-24
action_items: Alex Kim (Redwood SE) - Rerun p95 latency tests with batch_size=8, quantized model, keep KV cache warm; due 2025-02-18
Maya Patel (AE) - Share updated pricing delta + dedicated proposition; due 2025-02-17
Rachel Gomez (NimbleHealth) - Upload production sample traces & sequence length distribution; due 2025-02-16
Samir Rao (NimbleHealth) - Validate VPC network egress baseline and share network diagram; due 2025-02-20
Jordan Li (Redwood CSM) - Book production-like load window and invite attendees; due 2025-02-19
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-02-14 15:00 PST | Duration: 46 minutes | Attendees: Maya, Alex, Jordan (Redwood); Rachel, Samir, Priya, Tom (NimbleHealth partial)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everybody thanks for joining, quick agenda — run through week two benchmarks vs their baseline, call out any regressions, propose tuning, decide next steps. Sound good?
[00:12] Rachel: Yep, sounds good. We mostly want to see p95 numbers, the p50 is fine but p95 is what blows up in prod.
[00:18] Samir: And network egress matters, we have a 100ms baseline from region A to B that I'll surface later.
[00:25] Alex: Great, I'll jump into the numbers. Slide 1 of the sheet is the raw runs — note these were run against the 13B model variant, seq len 1024 for the historical run, and we mirrored the baseline provider's request pattern as closely as possible.
[00:40] Alex: p50 Redwood Dedicated -> 95 ms; p95 -> 420 ms. Baseline (SageMaker-ish) p50 -> 120 ms; p95 -> 760 ms. Throughput (tokens/sec) under steady 8 concurrent streams: Redwood 420 tok/s aggregate, Baseline 260 tok/s.
[01:05] Priya: That's pretty compelling on p95; what's the cost per 1k tokens difference?
[01:09] Maya: We ran a quick cost calc; raw inference compute cost (not infra) is about 0.32 USD per 1k tokens on Redwood optimized path vs 0.54 USD per 1k tokens on their baseline. I'll send the detailed delta.
[01:24] Samir: Are these runs using quantized weights? We need to compare apples to apples.
[01:29] Alex: The baseline we reproduced used fp16; our Redwood runs include both fp16 and int8 quantized variants. The numbers I just read were for fp16 on both sides, quantized yields lower latency but we had to tune batch_size to avoid quality degradation.
[01:45] Rachel: Any quality diffs observed when quantizing? We have a small eval set we care about.
[01:50] Alex: We ran quick BLEU-like scoring on the eval subset; int8 introduced a small 0.8% delta on our proxy score for a few prompts — most customers might not notice but your team should validate. We can run the exact eval set you provide.
[02:05] Priya: Okay please do that.
[02:08] Tom (brief): I'm on a tight call, can you flag any blockers?
[02:11] Maya: No blockers yet; main items are finalizing p95 runs in a production-like setup and confirming cost/latency at our committed capacity.
[02:20] Alex: Next slide shows latency distribution over time — you'll see warm vs cold differences. p95 spikes largely coincide with NV cache misses and KV cache cold starts at the start of a burst. With a warmed cache and continuous batching our p95 is stable around 400-420 ms.
[02:39] Rachel: How many concurrent requests were you running for the p95? Our production has bursts up to 120 concurrent short chat sessions.
[02:46] Alex: For these bench runs we did 8 long sessions to approximate throughput and later a burst test at 80 concurrent short sessions — in the 80-concurrency burst p95 rose to about 680ms on the baseline but Redwood stayed around 520ms with auto-batching enabled. Note the Redwood Dedicated setup had autoscaler set to maintain headroom for burst up to 100 sessions.
[03:12] Samir: Was the autoscaler reacting fast enough? We need to know the cold-start behavior when adding GPUs or pods.
[03:18] Alex: Autoscale in Dedicated is target-based; during the test we injected a sudden 3x load and saw a degradation window of about 35s where p95 trended up — after that it recovered to normal. That 35s is mostly warmup and model loading in the cluster. If you want zero-window we can discuss reserved burst capacity.
[03:37] Priya: Can we get a chart of that warmup curve?
[03:40] Jordan: I'll export the time-series and share it after the call.
[03:43] Rachel: Network variance — Samir mentioned region-to-region. How much of the p95 is network versus inference?
[03:49] Alex: We did host-local timings. Inference-only p95 on our side is about 380ms; end-to-end including our network baseline is 420ms. So network ~40ms in our runs. If you have a 100ms egress on your side we'd add that to end-to-end.
[04:05] Samir: Right that matches our measurements.
[04:08] Alex: On throughput: batching aggressively gives tokens/sec uplift but increases per-request latency slightly. For chat short-turn workloads we recommend batch_size=4-8, with continuous batching window of 20-40ms. For long completion workloads we can push batch to 12-16.
[04:25] Rachel: For our product most turns are ~64 tokens. So batch_size 8 seems safe.
[04:29] Alex: Good. The next thing we tested was KV cache pinning — when the same session continues, KV cache eliminates recompute and we saw p50 drop to 70ms and p95 to 210ms for subsequent tokens. That is where Redwood's continuous KV cache helps on threaded chat workloads.
[04:46] Priya: Are there any security tradeoffs with KV caching? We are in healthcare, so data handling is sensitive.
[04:52] Maya: We respect your security needs — Dedicated + Private options give you VPC and KMS integration. KV cache is ephemeral and never leaves the control plane when on Dedicated; we can provide the design note.
[05:02] Priya: Please share the note.
[05:05] Alex: Quick note on quality: when we bumped batch sizes and enabled int8 quant, we ran your eval set (proxy) and saw micro-deltas for a handful of prompts. We'll run the full eval you provide to certify no regressions.
[05:18] Rachel: Good. On costs, do the numbers assume autoscaling to zero?
[05:22] Maya: The cost calc here assumes mid-commit Dedicated with a reduced per-token compute cost; it doesn't assume autoscale-to-zero. If you want autoscale-to-zero your per-token would be slightly higher due to more frequent cold starts unless you accept reserved burst.
[05:36] Samir: We can't tolerate long cold starts. For the pilot we'd rather pay for some standing capacity.
[05:42] Maya: Noted — we'll add a reserved capacity option to the pricing sheet.
[05:46] Alex: Back to benchmarks, we also compared variance across different sequence lengths. For seq len 256, p95 is much lower — Redwood p95 ~180ms vs baseline ~320ms. For seq len 2048, both slow down but Redwood shows better scaling due to kernel selection optimizations.
[06:06] Priya: Do you have a chart per seq length?
[06:08] Alex: Yes, it's in the spreadsheet.
[06:10] Rachel: One operational question — how do we validate that a model variant fallback happens if the dedicated pool is saturated?
[06:15] Maya: We can configure a fallback policy that routes to a cost-optimized variant (smaller model or quantized) or to hosted capacity; we can demo routing in the production-like run.
[06:25] Samir: We'll want a test that simulates saturation and validates graceful degradation.
[06:29] Jordan: We'll add that to the load test plan.
[06:32] Alex: A couple gotchas in the runs — we observed occasional transcription mismatch in the logs where the client timeout was too low; please ensure your frontend has a 5s extra headroom for p95.
[06:45] Rachel: Noted.
[06:47] Priya: Anything surprising in the results?
[06:50] Alex: Two things: 1) Our kernel selection gives us better scaling at longer contexts which your use-case hits — you get more advantage than the baseline at seq len >1024. 2) p95 improvements are highly sensitive to KV cache warmup — so the real gains show once steady-state is achieved.
[07:06] Rachel: So for our pilot, we should focus on steady-state throughput and warm cache behavior.
[07:11] Maya: Agreed. Proposed next step: Alex reruns p95 runs with batch_size=8 + int8 quant to show cost/latency tradeoff and run your provided eval set end-to-end; Rachel to share eval and traces; Jordan to schedule production-like load test.
[07:25] Tom (CTO): If you haven't already, share the security pack and SOC 2 evidence for our infosec team.
[07:31] Maya: Yes will send SOC2 & ISO notes and KMS design doc after the call.
[07:36] Rachel: Timeline — we want final pilot results by end of next week so we can make an exec recommendation.
[07:42] Maya: That's doable.
[07:45] Alex: Any other questions?
[07:47] Priya: One more on observability — can we get token-level cost breakdown per route?
[07:52] Jordan: Yes, we can enable per-route cost telemetry for the pilot and share dashboards.
[07:56] Rachel: Perfect.
[07:58] Maya: Ok we'll recap in the notes and list the action items. Thanks everyone.
[08:03] End of transcript.
notes: Benchmarks run against 13B model variant, both fp16 and int8 evaluated
Warm cache dramatically improves p95; KV cache pinning recommended
Autoscaling cold-start window ~35s observed during 3x sudden load injection
